# Psalm 49 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Psalm 49 is a "wisdom psalm" — didactic rather than praise, prayer, or prophecy. It addresses the folly of trusting in riches and the certainty of death, while offering the hope of redemption by God. Spurgeon calls it a "didactic hymn" sung "to the accompaniment of his harp." Maclaren says it "touches the high-water mark of Old Testament faith in a future life." The psalm has two refrains (v.12 and v.20) and two Selah pauses.

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/ ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## vv. 1–2: The Universal Summons

> *"Hear this, all you peoples; listen, all inhabitants of the world, both low and high, rich and poor alike."*

- **Gill** notes the Hebrew for "inhabitants of the world" is literally "inhabitants of time" (*cheled*), signifying men whose lives are temporary. He sees this universal address as evidence that the psalm belongs to Gospel times, when the middle wall of partition between Jew and Gentile is broken down.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon** emphasises that "all men are concerned in the subject" — the laws of providence are the same in all lands. "Rich and poor must soon meet together in the grave, they may well be content to meet together now."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Ellicott** notes the Hebrew distinction between *benê-âdam* ("sons of Adam" = low/common men) and *benê-îsh* ("sons of Ish" = men of status), analogous to *homo* and *vir* in Latin.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) adds that the psalmist "hoped to guide those who were troubled about the wealth of the wicked."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 3: Wisdom and Understanding

> *"My mouth will impart wisdom, and the meditation of my heart will bring understanding."*

- **Gill** reads "wisdom" (plural "wisdoms" in Hebrew) as pointing to Christ, "who is so called" in Proverbs 1:20, and to the Gospel — "the wisdom of God in a mystery."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon** says the psalmist is not praising himself but extolling the divine Spirit speaking through him. "The Holy Spirit does not make us speak as Balaam's ass…but he first leads us to consider and reflect."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Guzik** contrasts this psalm with others: "Other psalms praise and pray to God; this psalm teaches wisdom and imparts understanding."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 4: The Proverb and the Riddle

> *"I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will express my riddle with the harp."*

- **Ellicott** explains the psalmist first listens to catch the inspiration before communicating it. The Hebrew *māshal* ("proverb/parable") has the root idea of similitude and was used of Balaam's prophecies and Job's eloquent speeches. The "dark saying" (*ḥîdâh*, "riddle") comes from a root meaning either "to tie" (a knotty point) or "to sharpen" (an incisive saying). "To open" the riddle means to propound it, not solve it.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **JFB (Jamieson, Fausset & Brown)** note that "parable" and "proverb" translate the same Hebrew word. They explain that "dark saying" or "riddle" indicates the composition is figurative and somewhat obscure, requiring careful attention — like Jesus' parables (Matthew 13:12–15).  
  **Source:** https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_049.cfm

- **Spurgeon:** "The writer was no mystic, delighting in deep and cloudy things, yet he was not afraid of the most profound topics…To win attention he cast his proverbial philosophy into the form of song."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Guzik** (citing Kidner) says the better translation of "dark saying" is "riddle" — the psalmist is not offering hidden mystical knowledge but things "simply difficult to understand and perceive."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 5: Why Fear?

> *"Why should I fear in times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround me?"*

- **Ellicott** renders "the iniquity of my heels" as "when iniquity dogs me at the heels" — wicked and prosperous men pursuing the psalmist with malice. He notes a possible allusion to Genesis 3:15 (the serpent bruising the heel), though not a direct reference.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **JFB** renders "iniquity of my heels" as literally "my supplanters" (cf. Genesis 27:36, Jacob the supplanter), meaning oppressors.  
  **Source:** https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_049.cfm

- **Gill** interprets "days of evil" broadly: days of old age, times of abounding iniquity and heresy, affliction and persecution, even the day of death and judgment. For the believer, none of these warrant slavish fear.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon**: "The man of God looks calmly forward to dark times…There can be no real ground of alarm to the faithful. Their enemies are too insignificant to be worthy of one thrill of fear."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## v. 6: Trusting in Wealth

> *"They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches."*

- **Guzik** stresses that Psalm 49 is not condemning wealth per se (Abraham and David were wealthy men who trusted God). The problem is *trusting* in wealth and *boasting* in riches — this is "simply idolatry." He offers diagnostic questions: "What loss in life would most trouble me — material or spiritual?"  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

- **Spurgeon** calls this a "rotten confidence" — "When we set our rock in contrast with theirs, it would be folly to be afraid of them."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## vv. 7–8: No Man Can Redeem Another

> *"No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice."*

- **Ellicott** says "brother" is used in the wide sense (as in Leviticus 19:17). Death is the debt all owe, and "no wealth can buy a man off. God…is not to be bribed." He explicitly states: "There is no anticipation of the Christian scheme of redemption from sin" here — "soul" (*nephesh*) means animal life, and the context is about ransom from death, not sin.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Gill**, by contrast, reads this Christologically: "the only price of redemption of the soul is the precious blood of Christ…nor is the redemption of the soul possible upon any other ground." He says the "brother" cannot be redeemed by human riches from "bondage to sin, Satan, and the law."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

- **Guzik** agrees: "Money itself can't rescue a soul because the redemption of their souls is costly — that is, beyond the ability of material things to purchase." He applies it to the substitutionary atonement fulfilled in Christ.  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

- **JFB**: "the ransom fails, the price is too precious, costly."  
  **Source:** https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_049.cfm

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** adds: "The gold is left behind forever, but not the soul! It lives on forever, in heaven's joys or hell's horrors."  
  **Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-49.html

**TRADITION DIFFERENCE:** Ellicott (Anglican) and the older critical commentators read vv.7–9 as about ransom from physical death only. Gill (Baptist), Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic), and Spurgeon (Baptist) read it as pointing toward Christ's atonement for the soul from sin and eternal death.

---

## v. 9: Live Forever, Not See Decay

> *"that he should live on forever and not see decay."*

- **Gill** says that even if a rich man lived "a thousand years twice told" (Ecclesiastes 6:6), he could not with all his riches redeem his brother; ultimately, eternal life "is not to be obtained by gold and silver, but is the pure gift of God."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon** wryly notes: "Mad are men now after gold, what would they be if it could buy the elixir of immortality?"  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- The "Pit" (Sheol) here, per **Guzik** (citing Trapp), is "more than just the grave, but the ultimate and empty destiny of those who reject God."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 10: Wise and Foolish Alike Die

> *"For it is clear that wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish and leave their wealth to others."*

- **Ellicott** corrects the AV division: the sense is "On the contrary he must see it [the grave]. Wise men must die…likewise the fool and the stupid must perish." Wealth cannot prolong life for anyone.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Gill** notes that even the wisest — Solomon, philosophers, physicians, spiritually wise teachers — all die. "The wise good man dies, but perishes not; he inherits eternal life; but the wicked fool and brute not only perish by death, but are punished with everlasting destruction in soul and body."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon:** "Folly has no immunity from death. Off goes the jester's cap, as well as the student's gown. Jollity cannot laugh off the dying hour."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## v. 11: Their Eternal Homes

> *"Their graves are their eternal homes — their dwellings for endless generations — even though their lands were their namesakes."*

- **Ellicott** notes that the LXX, Chaldee, and Syriac read *kibram* ("their graves") rather than the Masoretic *kirbam* ("their inward thought"), yielding: "Their graves are their homes, their dwelling places for ever." He says the last clause means either "they call the lands by their own names" or, following the LXX reading, "they are celebrated in their lands."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon**: "Common enough is this practice. His grounds are made to bear the groundling's name, he might as well write it on the water."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Guzik** (citing Trapp): "This is the ambition still of many, that take little care to know that their names are written in heaven; but strive to propagate them, as they are able, upon earth."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 12: First Refrain — Like the Beasts That Perish

> *"But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish."*

- **Ellicott** argues the reading of LXX and Vulgate ("without understanding" instead of "abideth not") should be adopted, bringing v.12 into exact correspondence with v.20. The Hebrew verb for "abideth not" (*yālîn*) means to lodge temporarily, not to dwell permanently. Thus: "Man, though in honour, without understanding, is like the beasts; they perish."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **JFB**: "However honored, man abideth not — literally, 'lodgeth not,' remains not till morning, but suddenly perishes as (wild) beasts, whose lives are taken without warning."  
  **Source:** https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_049.cfm

- **Guzik** (citing Boice): "It is the ability to think and reason that sets human beings apart from the remainder of creation. Yet how animal-like we are when we fail to consider the shortness of our days."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 13: The Fate of the Self-Confident

> *"This is the fate of the self-confident and their followers who endorse their sayings. Selah."*

- **Spurgeon** on "their way": "Their vain confidences are not casual aberrations from the path of wisdom, but their way, their usual and regular course; their whole life is regulated by such principles." On "their posterity": "Grace is not hereditary, but sordid worldliness goes from generation to generation. The race of fools never dies out."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Ellicott**: "This their way — i.e., the folly mentioned in the (amended) preceding verse…is a way of folly."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

---

## v. 14: Death Will Be Their Shepherd

> *"Like sheep they are destined for Sheol. Death will be their shepherd. The upright will rule them in the morning, and their form will decay in Sheol, far from their lofty abode."*

- **Ellicott** gives the literal rendering: "Like a flock for Sheol they are arranged; death is their shepherd." This is a ghastly parody of Psalm 23 — instead of the LORD shepherding the righteous to green pastures, Death shepherds the wicked to the grave. For "the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning," he suggests emending to "the upright shall go down to the grave amongst them until the morning" (when they will see light, contrast v.19).  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **JFB** renders "death shall feed on them" as "death shall rule them — as a shepherd," and "in the morning" as "suddenly, or in their turn."  
  **Source:** https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_049.cfm

- **Spurgeon**: "Death like a grim shepherd leads them on, and conducts them to the place of their eternal pasturage, where all is barrenness and misery…The poor saints were once the tail, but at the day break they shall be the head." He sees "the morning" as the resurrection morning.  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** takes "in the morning" as "the morning of the resurrection," when the upright shall have dominion.  
  **Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-49.html

- **Caryl** (cited in Spurgeon) asks, "Why like sheep? I answer, not for the innocency of their lives, but for their impotency in death…they could make no more resistance than a sheep can against a lion or a wolf."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

**TRADITION DIFFERENCE:** The interpretation of "the morning" divides commentators. The older critical tradition (Ellicott, and some modern scholars) tends to see it as "suddenly" or as a reference to the dawn after the night of death (with no necessary resurrection hope). Baptist and evangelical commentators (Spurgeon, Garner-Howes, Guzik) read it as the resurrection morning, when the upright will reign with Christ over the wicked.

---

## v. 15: God Will Redeem My Soul

> *"But God will redeem my soul from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself. Selah."*

- This is widely regarded as the theological high point of the psalm. **Guzik**: "The great *But God*…is one of the mountain-tops of Old Testament hope…it brings out into the open the assurance of victory over death which Ecclesiastes leaves concealed" (citing Kidner). Guzik also notes the word "receive" echoes Enoch: "God took him" (Genesis 5:24).  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

- **Spurgeon**: "No redemption could man find in riches, but God has found it in the blood of his dear Son. Our Elder Brother has given to God a ransom, and we are the redeemed of the Lord."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Ellicott** takes a more restrained view: "Taken by itself, this statement might only imply that when just at the point of death, the Divine favour would draw him back and rescue him." Yet he acknowledges that when combined with the preceding verse it represents "the dim foreshadowing of a better hope, that death did not altogether break the covenant bond between Jehovah and His people."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Coffman** calls this verse "the Old Testament equivalent of the New Testament instructions against the folly of trusting in material riches" and says it contains "one verse that outweighs all the others in the psalm put together."  
  **Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-49.html

- **Gill**: The redemption is by Christ, and "he shall receive me" means "he shall take me out of the tomb, take me up to heaven."  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/49.htm

---

## v. 16: Do Not Be Afraid When a Man Grows Rich

> *"Do not be amazed when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases."*

- **Guzik** notes the instruction "do not be afraid" addresses subtle fears: "Afraid because I think they prosper at my expense…because maybe God does not govern the universe as I believe He does…because maybe there is no reward for the righteous."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

- **Spurgeon**: "Let it not give thee any concern to see the godless prosper. Raise no questions as to divine justice…Temporal prosperity is too small a matter to be worth fretting about; let the dogs have their bones, and the swine their draff."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## v. 17: He Will Carry Nothing Away

> *"For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down."*

- **Spurgeon**: "Through the river of death man must pass naked. Not a rag of all his raiment, not a coin of all his treasure, not a joy of all his honour, can the dying worldling carry with him."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Guzik** contrasts: for the upright who look to God, "this world is the worst they will ever have it." For those trusting in riches, "this world is the best they will ever have it."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

---

## v. 18: The Self-Blessing Soul

> *"Though in his lifetime he blesses his soul — and men praise you when you prosper —"*

- **JFB** notes the literal Hebrew: "For in his life he blessed his soul" — a self-congratulation echoing the rich fool of Luke 12:19 and the rich man of Luke 16:25. "Men will praise thee, when thou doest well to thyself" — flatterers enhance the rich fool's self-complacency.  
  **Source:** https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_049.cfm

- **Spurgeon**: "The generality of men worship success, however it may be gained. The colour of the winning horse is no matter; it is the winner, and that is enough."  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## v. 19: He Will Join His Fathers, Never See Light

> *"he will join the generation of his fathers, who will never see the light of day."*

- **Ellicott** translates "who will never again look on the light," noting the implication of a contrast with a hope of resurrection for the upright.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon**: "Of all his treasures there remains not enough to furnish him one poor candle; the blaze of his glory is out for ever, and not a spark remains to cheer him. How then can we look with fear or envy upon a wretch doomed to such unhappiness?"  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

---

## v. 20: Final Refrain — Without Understanding

> *"A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish."*

- **Ellicott** notes that while v.12 (in the Masoretic text) reads "abideth not," v.20 reads "understandeth not" — and argues the LXX/Vulgate reading ("without understanding") should apply to both, making them an exact refrain. Understanding is what differentiates humans from beasts.  
  **Source:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/49.htm

- **Spurgeon** concludes with a solemn note: "Saddest of all is the reflection, that though men are like beasts in all the degradation of perishing, yet not in the rest which animal perishing secures, for, alas! it is written, 'These shall go away into everlasting punishment.'"  
  **Source:** https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps049.php

- **Guzik**: "The psalm ends by repeating the warning…Their honor in this world will not preserve them in the next."  
  **Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-49/

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: The man without God, "tho he have not God, live wickedly, shall go like his wicked fathers, they shall never see light again, that shines on the saints…but exist in darkness, abandoned of God, for ever and ever."  
  **Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-49.html

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

### The Meaning of v.14 ("the morning")

- **Baptist / Evangelical** (Spurgeon, Garner-Howes, Guzik): The resurrection morning when the upright will rule.
- **Anglican / Critical** (Ellicott, Pulpit): "Suddenly" or "in their turn"; possibly the dawn after death's night but not necessarily resurrection.

### The Redemption in vv.7–9 and v.15

- **Baptist / Pentecostal** (Gill, Guzik, Spurgeon): Read Christologically — pointing to Christ's atoning sacrifice as the only ransom for the soul.
- **Anglican / Critical** (Ellicott): Restrict the meaning to ransom from physical death; "no anticipation of the Christian scheme of redemption from sin." However Ellicott still sees v.15 as a "dim foreshadowing" of resurrection hope.

### The Scope of the Audience (vv.1–2)

- **Gill** (Baptist): Sees the universal address as proof the psalm "belongs to Gospel times" when the wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down. He reads the psalm through a New Covenant lens.
- **Ellicott** (Anglican): Reads it in its original Israelite wisdom context, drawing parallels with Deuteronomy 32:1 and other Hebrew Scripture calls to universal attention.
